cards.informal: Submultiplicativity: $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|\,\|B\|_F$ and $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|_F\,\|B\|$. Norm comparison: $\|A\| \le \|A\|_F \le \sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(A)}\,\|A\|$. Both norms are unitarily invariant, and $$\|A\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top A) = \sum_i \sigma_i^2.$$
cards.conclusion: $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|\,\|B\|_F$, $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|_F\,\|B\|$, $\|A\| \le \|A\|_F \le \sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(A)}\,\|A\|$ and $\|A\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top A) = \sum_i \sigma_i^2$

cards.informal: For Hermitian $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $\lambda_k(A)=\max_{\dim_{\mathbb C}S=k}\min_{x\in S,\|x\|=1}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)=\min_{\dim_{\mathbb C}S=n-k+1}\max_{x\in S,\|x\|=1}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)$. In particular the extreme eigenvalues are the extrema of the Hermitian Rayleigh quotient; the real symmetric specialization uses $x^\top Ax$.
hypotheses: $1\le k\le n$; dimensions are over $\mathbb C$ (or over $\mathbb R$ for the existing real specialization)
cards.conclusion: $\lambda_k(A)=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{\|x\|=1,x\in S}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)=\min_{\dim S=n-k+1}\max_{\|x\|=1,x\in S}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)$, with attained inner and outer extrema; $\lambda_{\max}$ and $\lambda_{\min}$ are the attained extrema of the Rayleigh quotient.

cards.informal: The general real Moore–Penrose inverse exists at every rank, is unique, and satisfies all four Penrose identities. It agrees with pinvL/pinvR when the respective Gram matrix is invertible. Its products are the orthogonal range projectors. Its norm is zero for the zero matrix and otherwise the reciprocal of the smallest positive singular value. For every A, $\|A^\dagger\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}((AA^\top)^\dagger)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, over arbitrary finite index types
Full-column or full-row rank is required only for the ordinary inverse formulas
cards.conclusion: $AA^\dagger A=A$, $A^\dagger AA^\dagger=A^\dagger$, $(AA^\dagger)^\top=AA^\dagger$, $(A^\dagger A)^\top=A^\dagger A$; the inverse is unique, and $\|A^\dagger\|=0$ when rank is zero, otherwise $1/\sigma_{\operatorname{rank}(A)}(A)$.

baseline_audit.informal: The general real Moore–Penrose inverse exists at every rank, is unique, and satisfies all four Penrose identities. It agrees with pinvL/pinvR when the respective Gram matrix is invertible. Its products are the orthogonal range projectors. Its norm is zero for the zero matrix and otherwise the reciprocal of the smallest positive singular value. For every A, $\|A^\dagger\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}((AA^\top)^\dagger)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, over arbitrary finite index types
Full-column or full-row rank is required only for the ordinary inverse formulas
baseline_audit.conclusion: $AA^\dagger A=A$, $A^\dagger AA^\dagger=A^\dagger$, $(AA^\dagger)^\top=AA^\dagger$, $(A^\dagger A)^\top=A^\dagger A$; the inverse is unique, and $\|A^\dagger\|=0$ when rank is zero, otherwise $1/\sigma_{\operatorname{rank}(A)}(A)$.

cards.informal: The largest Ritz value of $Q^\top AQ$ over $\mathcal K_q(A,b)$ is within $\varepsilon\lambda_1 + \lambda_1\big(\tfrac{2}{(1+\sqrt{2\gamma})^{q-1}}\big)^2\tfrac{\|b\|^2}{\langle u_1,b\rangle^2}$ of $\lambda_1$, $\gamma = \varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)$: the gap-free form via the Chebyshev amplifier.
hypotheses: $A \succeq 0$ symmetric with top eigenpair $(\lambda_1, u_1)$, $\langle u_1, b\rangle \ne 0$
cards.conclusion: some Ritz value $\theta$ of $Q^\top AQ$ satisfies $\lambda_1 - \theta \le \varepsilon\lambda_1 + \lambda_1\Big(\dfrac{2}{(1+\sqrt{2\gamma})^{q-1}}\Big)^2\dfrac{\|b\|^2}{\langle u_1, b\rangle^2}$
cards.review_note: PSD and nonzero top-eigenvector overlap are explicit. Krylov containment, rather than equality, suffices for the Ritz lower bound.

theorem exists_mem_krylovSpace_sub_rayleigh_le [Nonempty n] {A : Matrix n n ℝ}
    (hA : A.PosSemidef) {u : n → ℝ} (hu : A *ᵥ u = hA.isHermitian.eigenvalues₀ 0 • u)
    (hu1 : ‖WithLp.toLp 2 u‖ = 1) {ε : ℝ} (hε0 : 0 < ε) (hε1 : ε < 1) {b : n → ℝ}
    (hb : u ⬝ᵥ b ≠ 0) (q : ℕ) :
    ∃ y ∈ krylovSpace A b (q + 1), y ≠ 0 ∧
      hA.isHermitian.eigenvalues₀ 0 * ‖WithLp.toLp 2 y‖ ^ 2 - y ⬝ᵥ (A *ᵥ y) ≤
        (ε * hA.isHermitian.eigenvalues₀ 0 + hA.isHermitian.eigenvalues₀ 0 *
          (2 / (1 + √(2 * (ε / (1 - ε)))) ^ q) ^ 2 * ‖WithLp.toLp 2 b‖ ^ 2 / (u ⬝ᵥ b) ^ 2) *
            ‖WithLp.toLp 2 y‖ ^ 2

clauses.statement: Over any field and arbitrary finite matrix labels, the vector-relative minimal polynomial is monic, has natural degree equal to the Krylov grade, and is the unique monic annihilator of that degree.

A polynomial annihilates the starting vector exactly when the vector-relative minimal polynomial divides it; the native polynomial-module annihilator ideal is generated by that polynomial, including zero vectors.
The Krylov space has dimension min(q,grade), and its first q powers are independent exactly when q is at most the grade, over an arbitrary scalar field.
The grade-sized Krylov space is invariant under the matrix and every later Krylov space equals it.
The vector-relative minimal polynomial divides the operator minimal polynomial, so the grade is at most its degree and the operator minimal-polynomial degree is at most the ambient dimension.
Grade zero is equivalent to a zero starting vector, and an invertible matrix's inverse image of the starting vector belongs to the grade-sized Krylov space, including empty dimension.

cards.informal: The Arnoldi basis $Q_q = [q_1,\dots,q_q]$ is the Gram–Schmidt orthonormalisation of $b, Ab, \dots, A^{q-1}b$; $H_q = Q_q^\top A Q_q \in \mathbb R^{q\times q}$ and $\underline H_q = Q_{q+1}^\top A Q_q \in \mathbb R^{(q+1)\times q}$. A matrix is upper Hessenberg if $h_{ij} = 0$ for $i > j+1$. Characterisations: $Q_q$ has orthonormal columns spanning $\mathcal K_q(A,b)$ when $q \le \nu$, $H_q$ and $\underline H_q$ are upper Hessenberg, $h_{j+1,j} = \|(I - Q_jQ_j^\top)Aq_j\| \ge 0$ with equality iff $j \ge \nu$, and the basis is unique up to signs (implicit-Q uniqueness: positive subdiagonal fixes it).
hypotheses: for orthonormality and the Hessenberg sign/uniqueness statements: $q+1 \le \nu(A,b)$ (no breakdown)
The uniqueness comparison basis $\tilde Q$ is a graded Krylov basis: its first $j$ columns span $\mathcal K_j(A,b)$ for each $j$
cards.conclusion: $Q_q^\top Q_q = I$, $\operatorname{range}Q_q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$, $H_q$ and $\underline H_q$ upper Hessenberg with $h_{j+1,j} > 0$ for $j < \nu$; any graded Krylov basis $\tilde Q$ with orthonormal columns, $\tilde Q e_1 = b/\|b\|$ and $\tilde Q^\top A\tilde Q$ upper Hessenberg with positive subdiagonal equals $Q_q$

current_atlas_snapshot.informal: The Arnoldi basis $Q_q = [q_1,\dots,q_q]$ is the Gram–Schmidt orthonormalisation of $b, Ab, \dots, A^{q-1}b$; $H_q = Q_q^\top A Q_q \in \mathbb R^{q\times q}$ and $\underline H_q = Q_{q+1}^\top A Q_q \in \mathbb R^{(q+1)\times q}$. A matrix is upper Hessenberg if $h_{ij} = 0$ for $i > j+1$. Characterisations: $Q_q$ has orthonormal columns spanning $\mathcal K_q(A,b)$ when $q \le \nu$, $H_q$ and $\underline H_q$ are upper Hessenberg, $h_{j+1,j} = \|(I - Q_jQ_j^\top)Aq_j\| \ge 0$ with equality iff $j \ge \nu$, and the basis is unique up to signs (implicit-Q uniqueness: positive subdiagonal fixes it).
hypotheses: for orthonormality and the Hessenberg sign/uniqueness statements: $q+1 \le \nu(A,b)$ (no breakdown)
The uniqueness comparison basis $\tilde Q$ is a graded Krylov basis: its first $j$ columns span $\mathcal K_j(A,b)$ for each $j$
current_atlas_snapshot.conclusion: $Q_q^\top Q_q = I$, $\operatorname{range}Q_q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$, $H_q$ and $\underline H_q$ upper Hessenberg with $h_{j+1,j} > 0$ for $j < \nu$; any graded Krylov basis $\tilde Q$ with orthonormal columns, $\tilde Q e_1 = b/\|b\|$ and $\tilde Q^\top A\tilde Q$ upper Hessenberg with positive subdiagonal equals $Q_q$

cards.informal: If $Q$ has orthonormal columns with $\mathcal K_q(A,b) \subseteq \operatorname{range}Q$ and $H = Q^\top AQ$, then $p(A)b = Q\,p(H)\,Q^\top b$ for every $p$ with $\deg p < q$, and $Q^\top p(A)b = p(H)Q^\top b$ for $\deg p \le q$. If moreover $\operatorname{range}Q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$ with $q \le \nu$, the characteristic polynomial $\chi_H$ is the unique monic $p$ of degree $q$ minimising $\|p(A)b\|$.
hypotheses: $Q \in \mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with $Q^\top Q = I$ and $\mathcal K_q(A,b) \subseteq \operatorname{range}Q$; $H = Q^\top AQ$
for the minimality clause: $\operatorname{range}Q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$ and $q \le \nu(A,b)$
cards.conclusion: $p(A)b = Q\,p(H)\,Q^\top b$ for $\deg p < q$; $Q^\top p(A)b = p(H)\,Q^\top b$ for $\deg p \le q$; $\|\chi_H(A)b\| = \min\{\|p(A)b\| : p \text{ monic}, \deg p = q\}$ with $\chi_H(A)b \perp \mathcal K_q$
cards.review_note: The projected identity permits degree <=q; the lifted identity needs degree <q. Grade q controls uniqueness of the monic characteristic minimizer.

cards.informal: $\mathcal P_k^0 = \{p \in \mathbb R[x] : \deg p \le k,\ p(0) = 1\}$ and, for $S \subseteq \mathbb C$, $\varepsilon_k(S) = \inf_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\sup_{z\in S}|p(z)|$. For any $A$, every $x \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ has residual $b-Ax=p(A)r_0$ for some $p\in\mathcal P_k^0$, and every such polynomial residual has an affine-Krylov representative. If $A$ is invertible, membership of a specified $x$ is equivalent to this residual-polynomial condition, and $x-x_\star=p(A)(x_0-x_\star)$ when $Ax_\star=b$. $\varepsilon_k$ is antitone in $k$, monotone in $S$, attained for finite or compact $S$, and $\varepsilon_k([a,b]) = 1/T_k\big(\tfrac{b+a}{b-a}\big)$ for $0<a<b$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0$, $k \in \mathbb N$
Invertibility of $A$ is required only for the converse at a specified $x$ and the error-polynomial identity.

clauses.statement: Every affine-Krylov iterate has a degree-bounded residual polynomial with constant coefficient one, and every such polynomial has an affine-Krylov representative, for arbitrary real matrices.

For a specified iterate the residual-polynomial converse requires invertibility; the forward error-polynomial identity relative to a supplied exact solution needs no invertibility when the iterate lies in the affine Krylov space.
Residual minimax error is defined by an extended nonnegative uniform supremum over any complex set, decreases with the degree, increases with the domain, is at most one, and is zero on the empty set.

Every compact complex set, including finite and empty sets or sets with invisible coefficient directions, has an attaining real residual polynomial with the advertised degree and constant-coefficient constraints.
On a positive real interval embedded in the complex plane, the residual minimax value is exactly the reciprocal Chebyshev value, including degree zero.

baseline_audit.informal: $\mathcal P_k^0 = \{p \in \mathbb R[x] : \deg p \le k,\ p(0) = 1\}$ and, for $S \subseteq \mathbb C$, $\varepsilon_k(S) = \inf_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\sup_{z\in S}|p(z)|$. For any $A$, every $x \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ has residual $b-Ax=p(A)r_0$ for some $p\in\mathcal P_k^0$, and every such polynomial residual has an affine-Krylov representative. If $A$ is invertible, membership of a specified $x$ is equivalent to this residual-polynomial condition, and $x-x_\star=p(A)(x_0-x_\star)$ when $Ax_\star=b$. $\varepsilon_k$ is antitone in $k$, monotone in $S$, attained for finite or compact $S$, and $\varepsilon_k([a,b]) = 1/T_k\big(\tfrac{b+a}{b-a}\big)$ for $0<a<b$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0$, $k \in \mathbb N$
Invertibility of $A$ is required only for the converse at a specified $x$ and the error-polynomial identity.
baseline_audit.conclusion: $x-x_0\in\mathcal K_k(A,r_0)\Rightarrow\exists p\in\mathcal P_k^0,\ b-Ax=p(A)r_0$; every $p\in\mathcal P_k^0$ has such an affine-Krylov representative; if $A$ is invertible, the implication is an equivalence for a specified $x$; $\varepsilon_{k+1}(S)\le\varepsilon_k(S)$; $S\subseteq S^\prime\Rightarrow\varepsilon_k(S)\le\varepsilon_k(S^\prime)$; the infimum is a minimum for finite $S$; $\varepsilon_k([a,b])=1/T_k(\frac{b+a}{b-a})$

cards.informal:
$x_k$ is a GMRES iterate if $x_k \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ and $\|b - Ax_k\|_2 \le \|b - Ax\|_2$ for all $x \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$. u = 0$ at the grade $
u = 
u(A,r_0)$. For symmetric $A$ this is MINRES.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0$, $k \in \mathbb N$ (complex form: $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with the Hermitian inner product)
cards.conclusion: existence; uniqueness of $r_k$ (and of $x_k$ if $A$ invertible); $r_k \perp A\mathcal K_k$; $\|r_k\| = \min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\|p(A)r_0\|$; $\|r_{k+1}\| \le \|r_k\|$; $\|r_k\| = \min_y\|\,\|r_0\|e_1 - \underline H_ky\|$; $A$ invertible $\Rightarrow r_{\nu(A,r_0)} = 0$

cards.informal: If $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$ with $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)$, then the GMRES residual satisfies $$\frac{\|r_k\|}{\|r_0\|} \le \min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\|p(A)\| \le \kappa_2(V)\min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|.$$ For normal $A$ ($V$ unitary) the factor is $1$, and the bound is then sharp in the worst case over $r_0$ (Greenbaum–Gurvits, Joubert).
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $V \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ invertible, $\lambda \in \mathbb C^n$ with $A = V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)V^{-1}$ over $\mathbb C$
cards.conclusion: $\|r_k\| \le \|V\|_2\|V^{-1}\|_2\,\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\,\|r_0\|$ for every real $p \in \mathcal P_k^0$; for $A$ normal, $\|r_k\| \le \max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\,\|r_0\|$

cards.informal: $x_k^F$ is a FOM iterate if $x_k^F \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ and $b - Ax_k^F \perp \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$. It exists and is unique iff $H_k$ is invertible, and then $x_k^F = x_0 + \|r_0\|Q_kH_k^{-1}e_1$ and $r_k^F = -h_{k+1,k}\,(e_k^\top H_k^{-1}e_1)\|r_0\|\,q_{k+1}$. For symmetric positive definite $A$ the FOM iterate is the CG iterate.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0 \ne 0$, $1 \le k \le \nu(A,r_0)$, Arnoldi data $Q_k, H_k, h_{k+1,k}, q_{k+1}$

cards.informal: $W(A) = \{x^*Ax : x \in \mathbb C^n, \|x\| = 1\}$ for $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (for real $A$, of its complexification). clauses.statement: The numerical range is the quadratic-form image of the complex Euclidean unit sphere, compact in every finite dimension, includes the complex spectrum, and is contained in the spectral-norm closed disk; empty matrices have empty numerical range.
Affine scalar transformations give the affine image of the numerical range; unitary similarity preserves it; compression by any matrix with orthonormal columns only shrinks it.
In positive dimension the real projection of the numerical range is the interval between the extreme eigenvalues of the Hermitian part.
The numerical range of every finite complex matrix is convex (Toeplitz-Hausdorff), including empty dimension; a Bloch sphere proof establishes the two-dimensional compression case.
For every normal complex matrix the numerical range is exactly the convex hull of its complex spectrum, including repeated eigenvalues and empty dimension.

cards.informal: For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ write $s_k(x)=\sum_{i\le k}x_i^\downarrow$ for the sum of the $k$ largest entries. $x\prec_w y$ (weak majorization) iff $s_k(x)\le s_k(y)$ for $k=1,\dots,n$; $x\prec y$ iff moreover $s_n(x)=s_n(y)$. Characterisations: $x\prec y$ iff $x=Dy$ for a doubly stochastic $D$ iff $x\in\operatorname{conv}\{Py: P \text{ a permutation}\}$ (Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya); $x\prec y$ iff $\sum_i\varphi(x_i)\le\sum_i\varphi(y_i)$ for every convex $\varphi$; $x\prec_w y$ iff the same holds for every increasing convex $\varphi$.

cards.informal: For symmetric $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$ and $0\le k\le n$: $$\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(A)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top AQ): Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ Q^\top Q=I_k\},$$ attained at any $k$ orthonormal top eigenvectors (dually, the bottom $k$ sum is the minimum). For $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$: $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AV): U^\top U=V^\top V=I_k\}$. Corollary: $\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A+B)\le\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A)+\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(B)$, i.e. $\lambda(A+B)\prec\lambda(A)+\lambda(B)$, and $\sigma(A+B)\prec_w\sigma(A)+\sigma(B)$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, eigenvalues in decreasing order (`eigenvalues₀`)
Singular-value form: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $U\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}$, $V\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with orthonormal columns, $k\le\min(m,n)$
cards.conclusion: $\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top AQ)\le\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A)$ with equality for top eigenvectors; $\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AV)\le\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)$ with equality for top singular vectors

baseline_audit.informal: For symmetric $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$ and $0\le k\le n$: $$\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(A)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top AQ): Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ Q^\top Q=I_k\},$$ attained at any $k$ orthonormal top eigenvectors (dually, the bottom $k$ sum is the minimum). For $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$: $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AV): U^\top U=V^\top V=I_k\}$. Corollary: $\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A+B)\le\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A)+\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(B)$, i.e. $\lambda(A+B)\prec\lambda(A)+\lambda(B)$, and $\sigma(A+B)\prec_w\sigma(A)+\sigma(B)$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, eigenvalues in decreasing order (`eigenvalues₀`)
Singular-value form: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $U\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}$, $V\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with orthonormal columns, $k\le\min(m,n)$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top AQ)\le\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A)$ with equality for top eigenvectors; $\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AV)\le\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)$ with equality for top singular vectors

cards.informal: A norm on $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ is orthogonally (unitarily) invariant if $\|UAV\|=\|A\|$ for all orthogonal $U,V$. (von Neumann) These are exactly $\|A\|=\Phi(\sigma(A))$ for a symmetric gauge function $\Phi$ on $\mathbb R^{\min(m,n)}$, i.e. a norm invariant under permutations and sign changes. (Fan dominance) $\|A\|\le\|B\|$ for every orthogonally invariant norm iff $\|A\|_{(k)}\le\|B\|_{(k)}$ for every $k$, i.e. iff $\sigma(A)\prec_w\sigma(B)$.
hypotheses: $\|\cdot\|$ a norm on $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $\|UAV\|=\|A\|$ for orthogonal $U\in O(m)$, $V\in O(n)$
cards.conclusion: $\|A\|=\Phi(\sigma_1(A),\dots,\sigma_{\min(m,n)}(A))$ with $\Phi$ a symmetric gauge function, and conversely every symmetric gauge function defines such a norm; $\big(\forall\,\|\cdot\|\ \text{UI}:\ \|A\|\le\|B\|\big)\iff\forall k,\ \|A\|_{(k)}\le\|B\|_{(k)}$

baseline_audit.informal: A norm on $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ is orthogonally (unitarily) invariant if $\|UAV\|=\|A\|$ for all orthogonal $U,V$. (von Neumann) These are exactly $\|A\|=\Phi(\sigma(A))$ for a symmetric gauge function $\Phi$ on $\mathbb R^{\min(m,n)}$, i.e. a norm invariant under permutations and sign changes. (Fan dominance) $\|A\|\le\|B\|$ for every orthogonally invariant norm iff $\|A\|_{(k)}\le\|B\|_{(k)}$ for every $k$, i.e. iff $\sigma(A)\prec_w\sigma(B)$.
hypotheses: $\|\cdot\|$ a norm on $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $\|UAV\|=\|A\|$ for orthogonal $U\in O(m)$, $V\in O(n)$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\|A\|=\Phi(\sigma_1(A),\dots,\sigma_{\min(m,n)}(A))$ with $\Phi$ a symmetric gauge function, and conversely every symmetric gauge function defines such a norm; $\big(\forall\,\|\cdot\|\ \text{UI}:\ \|A\|\le\|B\|\big)\iff\forall k,\ \|A\|_{(k)}\le\|B\|_{(k)}$

cards.informal: For symmetric $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$: $(A_{11},\dots,A_{nn})\prec\lambda(A)$ (Schur), so $\sum_{i\in S}A_{ii}\le\sum_{i\le|S|}\lambda_i(A)$ for every index set $S$ and $\sum_i\varphi(A_{ii})\le\operatorname{tr}\varphi(A)$ for convex $\varphi$. Conversely (Horn) for every $d\prec\lambda$ there is a symmetric matrix with diagonal $d$ and spectrum $\lambda$ (a rotation of $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)$).
cards.conclusion: $\operatorname{diag}(A)\prec\lambda(A)$; and every $d\prec\lambda$ is $\operatorname{diag}(Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)Q^\top)$ for some orthogonal $Q$

cards.informal: For symmetric $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and every index set $J$ with $|J|=k$: $$\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j(A+B)\le\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j(A)+\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(B),$$ i.e. $\lambda(A+B)-\lambda(A)\prec\lambda(B)$. For singular values, $|\sigma(A+E)-\sigma(A)|\prec_w\sigma(E)$; hence $\|\operatorname{diag}(\sigma(A+E)-\sigma(A))\|\le\|E\|$ in every unitarily invariant norm, in particular $\sum_i|\lambda_i(A+E)-\lambda_i(A)|\le\|E\|_*$.

cards.informal: $A$ symmetric, $\|x\|=1$, $\rho=x^\top Ax$, $r=Ax-\rho x$. (a) For every $\mu\in\mathbb R$ some eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $|\lambda-\mu|\le\|Ax-\mu x\|$; $\|r\|=\min_\mu\|Ax-\mu x\|$. (b) (Kato–Temple) if $\delta>0$ and $\lambda$ is the only eigenvalue in $(\rho-\delta,\rho+\delta)$ then $|\lambda-\rho|\le\|r\|^2/\delta$. Also $\nabla_x\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}=\frac{2(Ax-\rho(x)x)}{x^\top x}$.
cards.conclusion: (a) $\min_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\lambda-\mu|\le\|Ax-\mu x\|$; (b) $|\lambda-\rho|\le\|r\|^2/\delta$; (c) $\|(I-P_\lambda)x\|\le\|r\|/\delta$

cards.informal: If $A=U_A\Sigma_AV_A^\top$ and $B=U_B\Sigma_BV_B^\top$ then $A\otimes B=(U_A\otimes U_B)(\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_B)(V_A\otimes V_B)^\top$, so its native domain-side singular-value multiset, including domain zeros, is the multiset of pairwise products of the two native domain-side lists (thin lists require the additional rectangular zero padding); hence $\|A\otimes B\|=\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A\otimes B\|_F=\|A\|_F\|B\|_F$, $\operatorname{rank}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{rank}A\cdot\operatorname{rank}B$, $(A\otimes B)^\dagger=A^\dagger\otimes B^\dagger$. For symmetric $A,B$ the eigenvalues of $A\otimes B$ are $\lambda_i(A)\lambda_j(B)$ and those of $A\otimes I+I\otimes B$ are $\lambda_i(A)+\lambda_j(B)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ (any `Fintype` indices; product index types)
cards.conclusion: $\sigma(A\otimes B)=\{\sigma_i(A)\sigma_j(B)\}$ as multisets; $\|A\otimes B\|=\|A\|\|B\|$; $\|A\otimes B\|_F=\|A\|_F\|B\|_F$; $\operatorname{rank}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{rank}A\operatorname{rank}B$; $(A\otimes B)^\dagger=A^\dagger\otimes B^\dagger$
cards.review_note: Domain-side singular-value multiplicities correctly include rectangular zero padding; thin-list pairwise products alone would be false.

  {Q : Matrix (Fin q) (Fin q) ℝ} (hA : NLAlib.IsSVD A U V) (hB : NLAlib.IsSVD B P Q) :

        Matrix.kroneckerMap (fun x1 x2 => x1 * x2) (NLAlib.rectDiag (NLAlib.singularValues A))

      (Matrix.kroneckerMap (fun x1 x2 => x1 * x2) V Q).transpose

cards.informal: Let $L\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, $M\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ be symmetric and $X\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$. (a) If $|\lambda_i(L)-\lambda_j(M)|\ge\delta>0$ for all $i,j$ then $\|LX-XM\|_F\ge\delta\|X\|_F$. (b) If the eigenvalues of $M$ lie in $[a,b]$ and those of $L$ lie outside $(a-\delta,b+\delta)$, $\delta>0$, then $\|LX-XM\|\ge\delta\|X\|$ (spectral norm; also Frobenius). The one-sided case $\lambda_{\max}(L)\le\alpha-\delta$, $\lambda_{\min}(M)\ge\alpha$ is the one used for top-$k$ subspaces.

cards.informal: $A,\hat A=A+E\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric. $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal with $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal with $\hat A\hat Q_i=\hat Q_i\hat\Lambda_i$. If $\sigma(\Lambda_1)\subseteq[a,b]$ and $\sigma(\hat\Lambda_2)\cap(a-\delta,b+\delta)=\emptyset$ with $\delta>0$, then $$\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|=\|\hat Q_2^\top Q_1\|\le\frac{\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|E\|}{\delta},$$ and the same with Frobenius norms. Top-$k$ corollary: with $Q_1,\hat Q_1$ top-$k$ eigenvectors, $\|\sin\Theta\|\le\|E\|/(\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(\hat A))$ when the denominator is positive. Population-gap form (Yu–Wang–Samworth): if $g=\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(A)>0$ then $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/g$ and $\|\sin\Theta\|\le2\|E\|/g$.
hypotheses: $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal, $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal, $\hat A\hat Q_2=\hat Q_2\hat\Lambda_2$
cards.conclusion: $\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|\le\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|/\delta\le\|E\|/\delta$ (also in $\|\cdot\|_F$); $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k+1})$

baseline_audit.informal: $A,\hat A=A+E\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric. $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal with $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal with $\hat A\hat Q_i=\hat Q_i\hat\Lambda_i$. If $\sigma(\Lambda_1)\subseteq[a,b]$ and $\sigma(\hat\Lambda_2)\cap(a-\delta,b+\delta)=\emptyset$ with $\delta>0$, then $$\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|=\|\hat Q_2^\top Q_1\|\le\frac{\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|E\|}{\delta},$$ and the same with Frobenius norms. Top-$k$ corollary: with $Q_1,\hat Q_1$ top-$k$ eigenvectors, $\|\sin\Theta\|\le\|E\|/(\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(\hat A))$ when the denominator is positive. Population-gap form (Yu–Wang–Samworth): if $g=\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(A)>0$ then $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/g$ and $\|\sin\Theta\|\le2\|E\|/g$.
hypotheses: $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal, $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal, $\hat A\hat Q_2=\hat Q_2\hat\Lambda_2$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|\le\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|/\delta\le\|E\|/\delta$ (also in $\|\cdot\|_F$); $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k+1})$

current_atlas_snapshot.informal: $A,\hat A=A+E\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric. $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal with $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal with $\hat A\hat Q_i=\hat Q_i\hat\Lambda_i$. If $\sigma(\Lambda_1)\subseteq[a,b]$ and $\sigma(\hat\Lambda_2)\cap(a-\delta,b+\delta)=\emptyset$ with $\delta>0$, then $$\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|=\|\hat Q_2^\top Q_1\|\le\frac{\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|E\|}{\delta},$$ and the same with Frobenius norms. Top-$k$ corollary: with $Q_1,\hat Q_1$ top-$k$ eigenvectors, $\|\sin\Theta\|\le\|E\|/(\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(\hat A))$ when the denominator is positive. Population-gap form (Yu–Wang–Samworth): if $g=\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(A)>0$ then $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/g$ and $\|\sin\Theta\|\le2\|E\|/g$.
hypotheses: $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal, $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal, $\hat A\hat Q_2=\hat Q_2\hat\Lambda_2$
current_atlas_snapshot.conclusion: $\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|\le\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|/\delta\le\|E\|/\delta$ (also in $\|\cdot\|_F$); $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k+1})$

NLAlib.singular_subspace_perturbation_bounds {m n k : ℕ} {A E : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) ℝ}
  {U Uhat : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin m) ℝ} {V Vhat : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ} (hA : NLAlib.IsSVD A U V)
  (hhat : NLAlib.IsSVD (A + E) Uhat Vhat) (hk : k ≤ min m n) :
  have U₁ := NLAlib.headColumns U ⋯;
  have V₁ := NLAlib.headColumns V ⋯;
  have Uhat₁ := NLAlib.headColumns Uhat ⋯;
  have Vhat₁ := NLAlib.headColumns Vhat ⋯;
  have T := Matrix.diagonal fun i => NLAlib.singularValues (A + E) ↑i;
  have R := A * Vhat₁ - Uhat₁ * T;
  have S := A.transpose * Uhat₁ - Vhat₁ * T;
  have δ := NLAlib.singularValues (A + E) (k - 1) - NLAlib.singularValues A k;
  have g := NLAlib.singularValues A (k - 1) - NLAlib.singularValues A k;
  R = -(E * Vhat₁) ∧
    S = -(E.transpose * Uhat₁) ∧
      max (NLAlib.specNorm R) (NLAlib.specNorm S) ≤ NLAlib.specNorm E ∧
        (0 < δ →
            max (NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles U₁ Uhat₁))
                  (NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles V₁ Vhat₁)) ≤
                max (NLAlib.specNorm R) (NLAlib.specNorm S) / δ ∧
              max (NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles U₁ Uhat₁))
                    (NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles V₁ Vhat₁)) ≤
                  NLAlib.specNorm E / δ ∧
                √(NLAlib.frobNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles U₁ Uhat₁) ^ 2 +
                      NLAlib.frobNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles V₁ Vhat₁) ^ 2) ≤
                  √(NLAlib.frobNorm R ^ 2 + NLAlib.frobNorm S ^ 2) / δ) ∧
          (0 < g →
              max (NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles U₁ Uhat₁))
                  (NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles V₁ Vhat₁)) ≤
                2 * NLAlib.specNorm E / g) ∧
            (k = 0 →
              NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles U₁ Uhat₁) = 0 ∧
                NLAlib.specNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles V₁ Vhat₁) = 0 ∧
                  NLAlib.frobNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles U₁ Uhat₁) = 0 ∧
                    NLAlib.frobNorm (NLAlib.sinePrincipalAngles V₁ Vhat₁) = 0)

cards.informal: $A,B=A+E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$. Identity: $$B^\dagger-A^\dagger=-B^\dagger EA^\dagger+B^\dagger B^{\dagger\top}E^\top(I-AA^\dagger)+(I-B^\dagger B)E^\top A^{\dagger\top}A^\dagger.$$ Bounds: if $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$ then $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\mu\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|$ with $\mu=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (and $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|_F\le\sqrt2\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|_F$); without the rank condition, $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\mu\max(\|A^\dagger\|^2,\|B^\dagger\|^2)\|E\|$. If $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$ and $\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|<1$: $\|B^\dagger\|\le\frac{\|A^\dagger\|}{1-\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|}$, and $\|AA^\dagger-BB^\dagger\|\le\min(\|A^\dagger\|,\|B^\dagger\|)\|E\|$.
cards.conclusion: the three-term identity; $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|$ (equal rank); $\|AA^\dagger-BB^\dagger\|\le\min(\|A^\dagger\|,\|B^\dagger\|)\|E\|$ (equal rank)

baseline_audit.informal: $A,B=A+E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$. Identity: $$B^\dagger-A^\dagger=-B^\dagger EA^\dagger+B^\dagger B^{\dagger\top}E^\top(I-AA^\dagger)+(I-B^\dagger B)E^\top A^{\dagger\top}A^\dagger.$$ Bounds: if $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$ then $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\mu\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|$ with $\mu=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (and $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|_F\le\sqrt2\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|_F$); without the rank condition, $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\mu\max(\|A^\dagger\|^2,\|B^\dagger\|^2)\|E\|$. If $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$ and $\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|<1$: $\|B^\dagger\|\le\frac{\|A^\dagger\|}{1-\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|}$, and $\|AA^\dagger-BB^\dagger\|\le\min(\|A^\dagger\|,\|B^\dagger\|)\|E\|$.
baseline_audit.conclusion: the three-term identity; $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|$ (equal rank); $\|AA^\dagger-BB^\dagger\|\le\min(\|A^\dagger\|,\|B^\dagger\|)\|E\|$ (equal rank)

cards.informal: For a square real or complex matrix, $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$ when $A$ is invertible and $\kappa_2(A)=\infty$ otherwise. The value lies in $\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\}$. On invertible matrices of positive dimension it equals the ratio of largest to smallest singular values; it is invariant under adjoint and inversion, and is at least one in positive dimension. For positive-definite real matrices it is the extreme eigenvalue ratio. For square invertible real matrices of positive dimension, the attained relative distance to singularity is $1/\kappa_2(A)$. The separate rectangular quantity `moorePenroseConditionNumber` is $\|A\|_2\|A^\dagger\|_2$, takes value zero at zero, and agrees with the real value of $\kappa_2$ on invertible square matrices.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb K^{n\times n}$ with $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ (`RCLike`), on a finite index type
The usual largest/smallest singular-value ratio requires invertibility and positive dimension; the lower bound $\kappa_2(A)\ge1$ requires nonempty indices
The eigenvalue-ratio and attained distance-to-singularity results are stated for real matrices of positive square dimension; the former assumes positive definiteness and the latter invertibility
The empty square matrix is invertible and has condition number zero; the separate Moore–Penrose quantity applies to rectangular matrices
cards.conclusion: $\kappa_2(A)=\infty$ exactly when $A$ is singular; otherwise $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$, equal to $\sigma_1(A)/\sigma_n(A)$ in positive dimension. For invertible real $A$ of positive dimension, $\min\{\|E\|_2/\|A\|_2:A+E\text{ singular}\}=1/\kappa_2(A)$.
cards.review_note: Uses the textbook extended condition number for square matrices and separates the Moore-Penrose product; empty square condition number is explicitly zero.

baseline_audit.informal: For a square real or complex matrix, $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$ when $A$ is invertible and $\kappa_2(A)=\infty$ otherwise. The value lies in $\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\}$. On invertible matrices of positive dimension it equals the ratio of largest to smallest singular values; it is invariant under adjoint and inversion, and is at least one in positive dimension. For positive-definite real matrices it is the extreme eigenvalue ratio. For square invertible real matrices of positive dimension, the attained relative distance to singularity is $1/\kappa_2(A)$. The separate rectangular quantity `moorePenroseConditionNumber` is $\|A\|_2\|A^\dagger\|_2$, takes value zero at zero, and agrees with the real value of $\kappa_2$ on invertible square matrices.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb K^{n\times n}$ with $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ (`RCLike`), on a finite index type
The usual largest/smallest singular-value ratio requires invertibility and positive dimension; the lower bound $\kappa_2(A)\ge1$ requires nonempty indices
The eigenvalue-ratio and attained distance-to-singularity results are stated for real matrices of positive square dimension; the former assumes positive definiteness and the latter invertibility
The empty square matrix is invertible and has condition number zero; the separate Moore–Penrose quantity applies to rectangular matrices
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\kappa_2(A)=\infty$ exactly when $A$ is singular; otherwise $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$, equal to $\sigma_1(A)/\sigma_n(A)$ in positive dimension. For invertible real $A$ of positive dimension, $\min\{\|E\|_2/\|A\|_2:A+E\text{ singular}\}=1/\kappa_2(A)$.
baseline_audit.review_note: Uses the textbook extended condition number for square matrices and separates the Moore-Penrose product; empty square condition number is explicitly zero.

For invertible $A$ and $\|A^{-1}E\|<1$: $A+E$ is invertible, $$\|(A+E)^{-1}\|\le\frac{\|A^{-1}\|}{1-\|A^{-1}E\|},\qquad\|(A+E)^{-1}-A^{-1}\|\le\frac{\|A^{-1}\|^2\|E\|}{1-\|A^{-1}E\|},$$ and $\|(A+E)^{-1}-A^{-1}\|_F\le\frac{\|A^{-1}\|^2\|E\|_F}{1-\|A^{-1}E\|}$.

cards.informal: Let $A$ be invertible, $Ax=b\ne0$, and $(A+\Delta A)(x+\Delta x)=b+\Delta b$ with $\kappa(A)\frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}<1$. Then $$\frac{\|\Delta x\|}{\|x\|}\le\frac{\kappa(A)}{1-\kappa(A)\frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}}\Big(\frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}+\frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|}\Big).$$ A posteriori: for any $\hat x$, $\frac{\|x-\hat x\|}{\|x\|}\le\kappa(A)\frac{\|b-A\hat x\|}{\|b\|}$.
cards.conclusion: $\|\Delta x\|/\|x\|\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\|\Delta A\|/\|A\|}(\|\Delta A\|/\|A\|+\|\Delta b\|/\|b\|)$ and $\|x-\hat x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa\|b-A\hat x\|/\|b\|$

cards.informal: Every $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$ factors as $A=QR$ with $Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $Q^\top Q=I_n$, and $R$ upper triangular with $R_{ii}\ge0$ (thin QR; a full QR has $Q$ orthogonal $m\times m$). If $\operatorname{rank}A=n$ then $R_{ii}>0$, the pair $(Q,R)$ is unique, $R^\top R=A^\top A$ (so $R^\top$ is the Cholesky factor of $A^\top A$), $QQ^\top$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{range}A$, $\sigma_i(R)=\sigma_i(A)$ and $\kappa(R)=\kappa(A)$.
cards.conclusion: $\exists Q,R$: $A=QR$, $Q^\top Q=I$, $R$ upper triangular with $R_{ii}\ge0$; unique with $R_{ii}>0$ under full column rank, and then $R^\top R=A^\top A$, $QQ^\top=AA^\dagger$, $\sigma(R)=\sigma(A)$

theorem qr_decomposition {m n : Type*} [Fintype m] [Fintype n]
    [DecidableEq m] [LinearOrder n] (A : Matrix m n ℝ)
    (hCard : Fintype.card n ≤ Fintype.card m) :
    ∃ Q : Matrix m n ℝ, ∃ R : Matrix n n ℝ,
      IsQR A Q R ∧ (∀ i, 0 ≤ R i i) ∧
        Rᵀ * R = Aᵀ * A ∧
        (∀ k, singularValues R k = singularValues A k) ∧
        moorePenroseConditionNumber R = moorePenroseConditionNumber A ∧
        (∀ e : n ↪ m, ∃ W : Matrix m m ℝ, ∃ T : Matrix m n ℝ,
          HasOrthonormalCols W ∧ W * Wᵀ = 1 ∧ W.submatrix id e = Q ∧
            W * T = A ∧ T.submatrix e id = R ∧
              (∀ i ∉ Set.range e, ∀ j, T i j = 0)) ∧
        (A.rank = Fintype.card n → (∀ i, 0 < R i i) ∧
          Q * Qᵀ = A * moorePenroseInverse A ∧
          ∀ (Q' : Matrix m n ℝ) (R' : Matrix n n ℝ),
            IsQR A Q' R' → (∀ i, 0 < R' i i) → Q' = Q ∧ R' = R)

current_atlas_snapshot.informal: Every $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$ factors as $A=QR$ with $Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $Q^\top Q=I_n$, and $R$ upper triangular with $R_{ii}\ge0$ (thin QR; a full QR has $Q$ orthogonal $m\times m$). If $\operatorname{rank}A=n$ then $R_{ii}>0$, the pair $(Q,R)$ is unique, $R^\top R=A^\top A$ (so $R^\top$ is the Cholesky factor of $A^\top A$), $QQ^\top$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{range}A$, $\sigma_i(R)=\sigma_i(A)$ and $\kappa(R)=\kappa(A)$.
current_atlas_snapshot.conclusion: $\exists Q,R$: $A=QR$, $Q^\top Q=I$, $R$ upper triangular with $R_{ii}\ge0$; unique with $R_{ii}>0$ under full column rank, and then $R^\top R=A^\top A$, $QQ^\top=AA^\dagger$, $\sigma(R)=\sigma(A)$

cards.informal: The $k$-th subspace iterate from a starting block $\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times s}$ is the subspace $\mathcal{S}_k = \operatorname{range}(A^k \Omega)$; any orthonormal $Q_k$ with $\operatorname{range} Q_k = \mathcal{S}_k$ is a basis the algorithm may carry, and the Ritz pairs are those of $Q_k^\top A Q_k$. Orthonormalisation does not change $\mathcal{S}_k$, and $\mathcal{S}_k \subseteq \mathcal{K}_{k+1}(A, \Omega)$ (block Krylov with the fixed polynomial $x^k$).
cards.conclusion: $\mathcal{S}_k = \operatorname{range}(A^k\Omega) \le \mathcal{K}_{k+1}(A,\Omega)$; the compression $Q_k^\top A Q_k$ is independent of the orthonormal basis $Q_k$ up to orthogonal similarity

cards.informal: Exact graph normalization gives actual complex principal-angle and individual eigenvector-angle bounds. Hermitian matrices use eigenvalue magnitudes, and individual initial factors are graph-column norms.
hypotheses: $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ has an orthonormal invariant eigenbasis split $[U_1\ U_2]$, with leading diagonal eigenvalues lambda_i and tail diagonal Lambda_2
Omega has s columns and $\Omega_1=U_1^*\Omega$ is invertible; $\Omega_2=U_2^*\Omega$, $F_0=\Omega_2\Omega_1^{-1}$, and $\mathcal S_t=\operatorname{range}(A^t\Omega)$
t>=0, alpha>0 and $|\lambda_i|\ge\alpha$; let $\beta=\|\Lambda_2\|$. Real matrices, indefinite spectra and empty trailing blocks are included
cards.conclusion: $\tan\theta_{\max}(\mathcal S_t,\operatorname{range}U_1)\le(\beta/\alpha)^t\tan\theta_{\max}(\operatorname{range}\Omega,\operatorname{range}U_1)$. For each $u_i=U_1e_i$, the actual Hilbert projection tangent obeys $\tan\angle(u_i,\mathcal S_t)\le(\beta/|\lambda_i|)^t\|F_0e_i\|$. This initial factor is not generally the initial vector-to-subspace tangent. For a PSD ordered spectrum alpha=lambda_s and beta=lambda_(s+1) recover the usual ratio; empty tails are exact.
cards.review_note: Magnitude bounds handle indefinite Hermitian spectra. The individual factors are graph-column norms rather than a shared scalar condition factor.

baseline_audit.informal: Exact graph normalization gives actual complex principal-angle and individual eigenvector-angle bounds. Hermitian matrices use eigenvalue magnitudes, and individual initial factors are graph-column norms.
hypotheses: $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ has an orthonormal invariant eigenbasis split $[U_1\ U_2]$, with leading diagonal eigenvalues lambda_i and tail diagonal Lambda_2
Omega has s columns and $\Omega_1=U_1^*\Omega$ is invertible; $\Omega_2=U_2^*\Omega$, $F_0=\Omega_2\Omega_1^{-1}$, and $\mathcal S_t=\operatorname{range}(A^t\Omega)$
t>=0, alpha>0 and $|\lambda_i|\ge\alpha$; let $\beta=\|\Lambda_2\|$. Real matrices, indefinite spectra and empty trailing blocks are included
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\tan\theta_{\max}(\mathcal S_t,\operatorname{range}U_1)\le(\beta/\alpha)^t\tan\theta_{\max}(\operatorname{range}\Omega,\operatorname{range}U_1)$. For each $u_i=U_1e_i$, the actual Hilbert projection tangent obeys $\tan\angle(u_i,\mathcal S_t)\le(\beta/|\lambda_i|)^t\|F_0e_i\|$. This initial factor is not generally the initial vector-to-subspace tangent. For a PSD ordered spectrum alpha=lambda_s and beta=lambda_(s+1) recover the usual ratio; empty tails are exact.
baseline_audit.review_note: Magnitude bounds handle indefinite Hermitian spectra. The individual factors are graph-column norms rather than a shared scalar condition factor.

cards.informal: An algorithm with matrix-vector access is an interaction tree: it is either an output, or a query vector $v$ with a continuation that receives $Av$ (adaptively). Its cost is the number of queries; its semantics on $A$ is obtained by answering every query with $Av$. A randomized algorithm is a tree-valued random variable. "$x_q$ is computable with $q$ matvecs" means some tree of cost $q$ outputs $x_q$ for every $A$; Gram–Schmidt and other work not touching $A$ is free.

cards.informal: $Q = [q_0,\dots,q_{q-1}]$ is a graded Krylov basis for $(A,b)$ if it has orthonormal columns and $\operatorname{span}(q_0,\dots,q_i) = \mathcal{K}_{i+1}(A,b)$ for every $i$. For $q \le \operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ it exists and is unique up to the sign of each column; $Q^\top A Q$ is unreduced upper Hessenberg, and a Jacobi matrix (symmetric tridiagonal with positive-or-negative nonzero off-diagonal) when $A$ is symmetric. $Q_{q}$ is the leading block of $Q_{q+1}$ and $T_q$ the leading principal submatrix of $T_{q+1}$.
cards.conclusion: existence; uniqueness up to $Q \mapsto Q D$ with $D$ diagonal $\pm1$; $Q^\top A Q$ unreduced Hessenberg, tridiagonal if $A = A^\top$; nesting of $Q_q, T_q$ in $Q_{q+1}, T_{q+1}$

cards.informal: For symmetric $A$ and an arbitrary graded orthonormal basis $q_j=p_j(A)b$, the polynomials are orthonormal for the spectral measure, and the compressed matrix is their Jacobi matrix. Its coefficients $\alpha_j=q_j^\top A q_j$ and signed $\beta_{j+1}=q_{j+1}^\top A q_j$ give the three-term recurrence; $|\beta_{j+1}|$ is the norm of the next residual. The characteristic polynomial obeys $\chi_jp_0=(\prod_{i=1}^j\beta_i)p_j$.

cards.informal:
Let $T_q=Q_q^	op A Q_q$ be the actual signed Lanczos compression, $M=\|b\|^2$ and $
u=\mu_b/M$. Its simple eigenvalues $	heta_i$ are the Gauss nodes, and $v_i(0)^2>0$ are the weights for $
u$; the original measure weights are $W_i=Mv_i(0)^2$. Thus $e_0^	op f(T_q)e_0=\sum_i v_i(0)^2f(	heta_i)$ and the original Gauss rule is $M$ times this value, with exactness through degree $2q-1$. For consecutive valid leading compressions, descending eigenvalues satisfy $	heta_i(T_{q+1})>	heta_i(T_q)>	heta_{i+1}(T_{q+1})$ for $0\le i<q$. The finite resolvent $r_q(z)=e_0^*(zI-T_q)^{-1}e_0$ is the Jacobi convergent of the normalized Stieltjes transform $\int(z-t)^{-1}\,d
u(t)$, and $Mr_q(z)=\sigma_q(z)/\chi_q(z)=\sum_i W_i/(z-	heta_i)$ off the actual node spectrum. The ordinary nested continued fraction is valid when every intermediate denominator is nonzero, in particular for nonreal $z$ or real $z$ above the spectrum. At real intermediate poles use the trailing/full determinant quotient, or the rational-function interpretation. For the actual polynomials $p_j$ orthonormal for $\mu_b$ and signed coupling $a_m$, $(x-y)\sum_{j<m}p_j(x)p_j(y)=a_m(p_m(x)p_{m-1}(y)-p_{m-1}(x)p_m(y))$. This multiplied identity holds for all $x,y$; division requires $x
e y$, and formal differentiation gives the positive confluent kernel. If the top monic norm is zero, use the monic Wronskian divided by $h_{m-1}$ instead of a nonexistent normalized $p_m$. At order zero the scalar approximant is zero and the empty characteristic denominator is one.
hypotheses: $A$ is real symmetric, $b\ne0$, $1\le q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$, and $T_q$ is the actual compression of a graded Lanczos basis. The spectral measure $\mu_b$ has original mass $M=\|b\|^2$; squared first eigenvector coordinates integrate $\mu_b/M$.

Strict interlacing compares a size-$(q+1)$ decomposition with its leading size-$q$ restriction, so $q+1\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ is required. The larger order may equal the grade; eigenvalues above are ordered nonincreasingly.

The normalized Christoffel–Darboux formula from a size-$q$ decomposition uses $1\le m<q$. A fully normalized top polynomial requires $h_m>0$; the monic norm-divided terminal formula requires only the preceding norms $h_0,\ldots,h_{m-1}>0$.

The ordinary complex resolvent and determinant quotient require $z\notin\operatorname{spec}(T_q)$. Literal nested division additionally requires every trailing-block determinant to be nonzero; this is derived for nonreal $z$ and for real $z$ above the spectrum. The divided kernel requires $x\ne y$; multiplied and confluent formulas cover the other cases.
Zero order is handled by the empty determinant and zero scalar fraction, with no first coordinate or normalized zero-mass measure.
cards.conclusion: The actual Jacobi/Lanczos matrix gives simple Gauss nodes and positive normalized weights, original-mass quadrature exactness, strict consecutive interlacing, finite complex resolvent and continued-fraction identities, and multiplied/divided/confluent Christoffel–Darboux identities on their stated finite-order domains.
cards.review_note: For q≥1, squared first eigenvector coordinates are positive Gauss weights for μ_b/M, with M=‖b‖²; multiplication by M gives the original-measure rule and finite second-kind approximant. Consecutive valid leading compressions strictly interlace in descending order θ_i(T_(q+1))>θ_i(T_q)>θ_(i+1)(T_(q+1)), requiring q+1≤grade. Signed normalized CD uses 1≤m<q. A monic norm-divided kernel permits a zero-norm top polynomial when preceding norms are positive. Actual characteristic continuants and off-spectrum complex resolvents are proved. Ordinary nested fractions require every intermediate denominator nonzero, derived for nonreal shifts and the existing real-above-spectrum branch.

current_atlas_snapshot.informal:
Let $T_q=Q_q^	op A Q_q$ be the actual signed Lanczos compression, $M=\|b\|^2$ and $
u=\mu_b/M$. Its simple eigenvalues $	heta_i$ are the Gauss nodes, and $v_i(0)^2>0$ are the weights for $
u$; the original measure weights are $W_i=Mv_i(0)^2$. Thus $e_0^	op f(T_q)e_0=\sum_i v_i(0)^2f(	heta_i)$ and the original Gauss rule is $M$ times this value, with exactness through degree $2q-1$. For consecutive valid leading compressions, descending eigenvalues satisfy $	heta_i(T_{q+1})>	heta_i(T_q)>	heta_{i+1}(T_{q+1})$ for $0\le i<q$. The finite resolvent $r_q(z)=e_0^*(zI-T_q)^{-1}e_0$ is the Jacobi convergent of the normalized Stieltjes transform $\int(z-t)^{-1}\,d
u(t)$, and $Mr_q(z)=\sigma_q(z)/\chi_q(z)=\sum_i W_i/(z-	heta_i)$ off the actual node spectrum. The ordinary nested continued fraction is valid when every intermediate denominator is nonzero, in particular for nonreal $z$ or real $z$ above the spectrum. At real intermediate poles use the trailing/full determinant quotient, or the rational-function interpretation. For the actual polynomials $p_j$ orthonormal for $\mu_b$ and signed coupling $a_m$, $(x-y)\sum_{j<m}p_j(x)p_j(y)=a_m(p_m(x)p_{m-1}(y)-p_{m-1}(x)p_m(y))$. This multiplied identity holds for all $x,y$; division requires $x
e y$, and formal differentiation gives the positive confluent kernel. If the top monic norm is zero, use the monic Wronskian divided by $h_{m-1}$ instead of a nonexistent normalized $p_m$. At order zero the scalar approximant is zero and the empty characteristic denominator is one.
hypotheses: $A$ is real symmetric, $b\ne0$, $1\le q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$, and $T_q$ is the actual compression of a graded Lanczos basis. The spectral measure $\mu_b$ has original mass $M=\|b\|^2$; squared first eigenvector coordinates integrate $\mu_b/M$.

Strict interlacing compares a size-$(q+1)$ decomposition with its leading size-$q$ restriction, so $q+1\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ is required. The larger order may equal the grade; eigenvalues above are ordered nonincreasingly.

The normalized Christoffel–Darboux formula from a size-$q$ decomposition uses $1\le m<q$. A fully normalized top polynomial requires $h_m>0$; the monic norm-divided terminal formula requires only the preceding norms $h_0,\ldots,h_{m-1}>0$.

The ordinary complex resolvent and determinant quotient require $z\notin\operatorname{spec}(T_q)$. Literal nested division additionally requires every trailing-block determinant to be nonzero; this is derived for nonreal $z$ and for real $z$ above the spectrum. The divided kernel requires $x\ne y$; multiplied and confluent formulas cover the other cases.
Zero order is handled by the empty determinant and zero scalar fraction, with no first coordinate or normalized zero-mass measure.
current_atlas_snapshot.conclusion: The actual Jacobi/Lanczos matrix gives simple Gauss nodes and positive normalized weights, original-mass quadrature exactness, strict consecutive interlacing, finite complex resolvent and continued-fraction identities, and multiplied/divided/confluent Christoffel–Darboux identities on their stated finite-order domains.

reviewed_clauses.statement: The actual canonical moment Jacobi compression has monic alpha diagonal and positive square-root monic-beta adjacent entries, and its normalized polynomials satisfy the corresponding three-term recurrence. Actual signed Lanczos T has its own diagonal and signed off-diagonal coefficient matrix.

At q≥1 and mass M=‖b‖²>0, first eigenvector-coordinate squares are positive normalized μ_b/M Gauss weights; multiplication by M restores original-measure exactness through degree 2q−1. Actual Lanczos polynomials themselves remain orthonormal for μ_b.
A valid size-(q+1) decomposition requires q+1≤grade; its descending spectra satisfy θ_i(T_(q+1))>θ_i(T_q)>θ_(i+1)(T_(q+1)). The larger order may equal the grade.

Actual signed normalized multiplied/confluent CD uses 1≤m<q. Monic norm-divided kernels need preceding positive norms and allow a zero-norm top polynomial; fully normalized top kernels additionally need h_m>0.

The actual nonreal Jacobi resolvent is the literal nested complex fraction for arbitrary signed real coefficients, and every intermediate scalar Schur denominator is proved nonzero. The actual signed Lanczos matrix inherits this formula.

The totalized Cramer determinant quotient holds at every shift; an ordinary analytic resolvent requires a nonzero final determinant. It handles real intermediate tail poles off the final spectrum, and continuants equal every leading characteristic polynomial.

Original mass times the actual finite canonical Jacobi resolvent equals the second-kind ratio and original Gauss partial fraction off the actual nodes; rooted moments match through degree 2n−1, including termination. The unscaled resolvent is the normalized-measure approximant, not the full nonterminal transform.
At order zero the scalar approximant is zero and the empty characteristic denominator is one; no nonexistent first coordinate is used.

cards.exact_scope: The finite unscaled resolvent is the normalized-measure approximant, not the full nonterminal Stieltjes transform. An ordinary resolvent requires the final shift off the spectrum. The totalized Cramer identity also holds at spectral poles but is not an analytic resolvent there. Real intermediate tail poles are handled by the final pole-free determinant quotient. Fully normalized top kernels require a positive top norm; divided CD requires x≠y. Order zero has scalar fraction zero and empty determinant one, without a first coordinate or normalized zero-mass measure.

Richardson and Chebyshev iteration are instances with explicit $s$.

cards.informal: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ invertible has a factorization $A = LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular iff every leading principal minor $\det A_{1..k,1..k}$ is nonzero; the factorization is then unique. One elimination step is the Schur complement: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ b/a & I\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a & c^\top \\ 0 & C - b c^\top/a\end{pmatrix}$.
hypotheses: $A$ invertible (for the iff); or just: all leading principal minors nonzero (for existence)
cards.conclusion: $\exists!\,(L, U)$ with $A = LU$, $L$ unit lower, $U$ upper triangular

cards.informal: The Cholesky recursion ($a \mapsto \sqrt a$, $b \mapsto b/\sqrt a$, continue on the Schur complement $C - bb^\top/a$) succeeds (every pivot $> 0$) iff $A$ is positive definite (for symmetric $A$); on success $L L^\top = A$ with $L$ lower triangular with positive diagonal, and $L$ is unique. For positive semidefinite $A$, pivoted (diagonal-pivoting) Cholesky never fails, stops after $\operatorname{rank} A$ steps and returns $L L^\top = A$.
cards.conclusion: $\mathrm{CholeskySucceeds}\,A \iff A \succ 0$; success $\Rightarrow$ `IsCholesky A (cholesky A)`; PSD: pivoted variant terminates at the rank

baseline_audit.informal: Classical and modified Gram–Schmidt on the columns of $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, as recursions, produce $Q$ with orthonormal columns and upper triangular $R$ with $A = QR$ and $r_{jj} > 0$; step $k$ breaks down iff $a_k \in \operatorname{span}(a_1,\dots,a_{k-1})$ (in exact arithmetic CGS and MGS give the same $Q, R$). $Q$ is the graded orthonormal basis of the column flag.
hypotheses: $A$ with linearly independent columns (for no breakdown)
baseline_audit.conclusion: $A = QR$, $Q^\top Q = I$, $R$ upper triangular with positive diagonal; breakdown at $k \iff \operatorname{rank} A_{:,1..k} < k$

cards.informal: $H_v = I - 2 v v^\top / (v^\top v)$ for $v \ne 0$ ($H_0 = I$): $H_v^\top = H_v$, $H_v^2 = I$, $H_v v = -v$, $H_v$ fixes $v^\perp$. With $v = x + \operatorname{sign}(x_1)\|x\| e_1$, $H_v x = -\operatorname{sign}(x_1)\|x\| e_1$.
cards.conclusion: $H_v$ orthogonal symmetric involution; $H_v x = \mp \|x\| e_1$ for the standard choice of $v$
cards.review_note: The actual Householder reduction uses householderSign(t)=1 for t>=0 and -1 otherwise. This chosen nonzero sign convention, including t=0, gives the reflector reduction; ordinary real sign(0)=0 would invalidate it for a nonzero vector whose first coordinate is zero.

cards.conclusion: $A = QR$, $Q$ orthogonal as a product of reflectors, $R$ upper triangular

baseline_audit.informal: A Givens rotation $G(i,j,\theta)$ is the identity except for the $2\times2$ rotation block in rows/columns $i,j$; it is orthogonal and can zero one chosen entry. An upper Hessenberg $H$ has $H = QR$ with $Q$ a product of $n-1$ rotations; $RQ$ is again upper Hessenberg (tridiagonal if $H$ is symmetric tridiagonal).
baseline_audit.conclusion: $G$ orthogonal; $G x$ zeroes $x_j$; Hessenberg QR in $n-1$ rotations; $RQ$ Hessenberg

cards.informal: For $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ there is orthogonal $Q$ with $Q^\top A Q = H$ upper Hessenberg, constructed by $n-2$ Householder reflectors; if $A$ is symmetric, $H$ is symmetric tridiagonal. When the first column of $Q$ is fixed and $H$ is unreduced, $Q$ and $H$ are determined up to signs (implicit Q theorem), and the columns of $Q$ form the Arnoldi basis of $(A, q_1)$.
cards.conclusion: $Q^\top A Q = H$ upper Hessenberg; symmetric $\Rightarrow$ tridiagonal; implicit Q uniqueness
cards.review_note: Actual Householder Hessenberg realization, orthonormal similarity, Hermitian tridiagonality and implicit-Q sign uniqueness are proved. These statements do not by themselves identify the columns as an Arnoldi basis for the supplied initial vector.

cards.informal: $x$ minimises $\|Ax - b\|_2$ iff $A^\top A x = A^\top b$ iff $r = b - Ax \perp \operatorname{range} A$; the minimiser is unique iff $A$ has full column rank, and then $x = A^\dagger b = R^{-1} Q^\top b$ for a thin QR $A = QR$, with $\|r\|^2 = \|b\|^2 - \|Q^\top b\|^2$.
cards.conclusion: minimiser $\iff$ normal equations $\iff$ residual orthogonal to $\operatorname{range} A$; unique iff full column rank; $x = A^\dagger b = R^{-1}Q^\top b$

baseline_audit.informal: $x$ minimises $\|Ax - b\|_2$ iff $A^\top A x = A^\top b$ iff $r = b - Ax \perp \operatorname{range} A$; the minimiser is unique iff $A$ has full column rank, and then $x = A^\dagger b = R^{-1} Q^\top b$ for a thin QR $A = QR$, with $\|r\|^2 = \|b\|^2 - \|Q^\top b\|^2$.
baseline_audit.conclusion: minimiser $\iff$ normal equations $\iff$ residual orthogonal to $\operatorname{range} A$; unique iff full column rank; $x = A^\dagger b = R^{-1}Q^\top b$

cards.informal: For symmetric $A$ with $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| \ge \dots$ and $u_1^\top x_0 \ne 0$: the normalised iterates $x_k = A^k x_0 / \|A^k x_0\|$ satisfy $\tan\theta(x_k, u_1) \le (|\lambda_2|/|\lambda_1|)^k \tan\theta(x_0, u_1)$ and $|\rho(x_k) - \lambda_1| \le (\lambda_1 - \lambda_n)\tan^2\theta(x_k,u_1)$, i.e. the Rayleigh quotient converges at rate $(|\lambda_2|/|\lambda_1|)^{2k}$.
cards.conclusion: $\tan^2\theta(x_k,u_1) \le (\lambda_2/\lambda_1)^{2k}\tan^2\theta(x_0,u_1)$; $|\rho(x_k) - \lambda_1| = O((\lambda_2/\lambda_1)^{2k})$
cards.review_note: The actual power-iteration Rayleigh bound orders the dominant eigenvalue by modulus and takes D at least every absolute distance from that eigenvalue. Spectral diameter is an admissible D. A signed lambda_1-lambda_n expression can be negative when the dominant eigenvalue is negative and is not the asserted absolute-error bound.

baseline_audit.informal: For symmetric $A$ with $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| \ge \dots$ and $u_1^\top x_0 \ne 0$: the normalised iterates $x_k = A^k x_0 / \|A^k x_0\|$ satisfy $\tan\theta(x_k, u_1) \le (|\lambda_2|/|\lambda_1|)^k \tan\theta(x_0, u_1)$ and $|\rho(x_k) - \lambda_1| \le (\lambda_1 - \lambda_n)\tan^2\theta(x_k,u_1)$, i.e. the Rayleigh quotient converges at rate $(|\lambda_2|/|\lambda_1|)^{2k}$.

findings.finding: The dominant eigenvalue is ordered by modulus, so lambda1-lambdan need not be nonnegative. The Lean theorem correctly takes D>=all absolute distances to the selected eigenvalue; use spectral diameter lambdaMax-lambdaMin or this D.

cards.informal: Inertia (numbers of positive, negative, zero eigenvalues) is invariant under congruence $A \mapsto X^\top A X$ with $X$ invertible. Consequently, for symmetric $A$ with $A - xI = L D L^\top$, the number of eigenvalues of $A$ less than $x$ equals the number of negative entries of $D$; for unreduced symmetric tridiagonal $T$ the number of sign changes in the Sturm sequence $\det(T_k - xI)$ counts the eigenvalues below $x$ (bisection).
hypotheses: $A$ symmetric; $X$ invertible; for the count, $LDL^\top$ of $A - xI$ exists (or the Sturm sequence has no zero)
cards.conclusion: $\operatorname{In}(X^\top A X) = \operatorname{In}(A)$; $\#\{\lambda_i < x\} = \#\{d_i < 0\}$

cards.informal: Starting from $u_1 = b/\|b\|$, the recursion $A^\top u_k = \beta_{k-1} v_{k-1} + \alpha_k v_k$, $A v_k = \alpha_k u_k + \beta_k u_{k+1}$ produces orthonormal $U_k, V_k$ and lower bidiagonal $B_k$ with $A V_k = U_{k+1} \underline{B}_k$ and $A^\top U_{k+1} = V_k \underline{B}_k^\top + \alpha_{k+1} v_{k+1} e_{k+1}^\top$; $V_k$ is the Lanczos basis of $(A^\top A, A^\top b)$ and $U_k$ that of $(AA^\top, b)$, with $B_k^\top B_k$ the Lanczos tridiagonal of $A^\top A$.
cards.conclusion: $AV_k = U_{k+1}\underline{B}_k$; $V_k$ = graded Krylov basis of $(A^\top A, A^\top b)$; $B_k^\top B_k = T_k(A^\top A)$

resolved_final_documentation_findings.finding: A zero input/output coordinate does not force the entire total componentwise condition number to zero: f=id on R^2 and x=(0,1) gives diag(0,1) of norm 1. The nonzero-coordinate condition is for relative interpretation; the parent has been asked to correct the misleading zero-fallback doc sentence.
resolved_final_documentation_findings.resolution: The parent corrected the current MapConditioning docstring to state total coordinatewise division and that a zero coordinate does not force the full norm to vanish.

cards.informal: Every $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ is $A=UTU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $T$ upper triangular, the eigenvalues on the diagonal in any prescribed order; a real $A$ is $A=QTQ^\top$ with $Q$ real orthogonal and $T$ real upper quasitriangular ($1\times1$ real blocks and general $2\times2$ real blocks for conjugate eigenvalue pairs), and $T$ can be taken triangular when all eigenvalues are real. Consequences: Schur's inequality $\sum_i|\lambda_i|^2=\|A\|_F^2-\|N\|_F^2\le\|A\|_F^2$ ($N$ the strictly upper part, equality iff $A$ normal); matrices with distinct eigenvalues are dense; over $\mathbb C$, over $\mathbb C$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ some similarity makes $A$ triangular with off-diagonal entries at most $\varepsilon$. Pencil version (QZ): $A=VT_AW^*$, $B=VT_BW^*$ simultaneously.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ (real Schur form) or $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (complex Schur form)
prescribed ordering of the eigenvalues for the complex form
cards.conclusion: $\exists$ orthogonal $Q$ (unitary $U$), quasitriangular (triangular) $T$: $A=QTQ^\top$; $\sum|\lambda_i|^2\le\|A\|_F^2$ with equality iff $A$ is normal
cards.review_note: General real 2x2 Schur blocks are used, rather than normal-only rotation-dilation blocks. Arbitrarily small triangular entries are the complex statement; real variant requires real spectrum.

baseline_audit.informal: Every $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ is $A=UTU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $T$ upper triangular, the eigenvalues on the diagonal in any prescribed order; a real $A$ is $A=QTQ^\top$ with $Q$ real orthogonal and $T$ real upper quasitriangular ($1\times1$ real blocks and general $2\times2$ real blocks for conjugate eigenvalue pairs), and $T$ can be taken triangular when all eigenvalues are real. Consequences: Schur's inequality $\sum_i|\lambda_i|^2=\|A\|_F^2-\|N\|_F^2\le\|A\|_F^2$ ($N$ the strictly upper part, equality iff $A$ normal); matrices with distinct eigenvalues are dense; over $\mathbb C$, over $\mathbb C$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ some similarity makes $A$ triangular with off-diagonal entries at most $\varepsilon$. Pencil version (QZ): $A=VT_AW^*$, $B=VT_BW^*$ simultaneously.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ (real Schur form) or $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (complex Schur form)
prescribed ordering of the eigenvalues for the complex form
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\exists$ orthogonal $Q$ (unitary $U$), quasitriangular (triangular) $T$: $A=QTQ^\top$; $\sum|\lambda_i|^2\le\|A\|_F^2$ with equality iff $A$ is normal
baseline_audit.review_note: General real 2x2 Schur blocks are used, rather than normal-only rotation-dilation blocks. Arbitrarily small triangular entries are the complex statement; real variant requires real spectrum.

A real normal matrix is real orthogonally similar to a direct sum of $1\times1$ blocks and $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$ (skew-symmetric and orthogonal matrices as special cases). Fuglede–Putnam: for normal $A,B$, $AX=XB\iff A^*X=XB^*$.

cards.informal: $A$ is diagonalizable if $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ with $\Lambda$ diagonal, equivalently it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, equivalently every eigenvalue has equal geometric and algebraic multiplicity (nondefective). $n$ distinct eigenvalues suffice; a direct sum is diagonalizable iff each summand is; two diagonalizations differ by an invertible block-diagonal factor on the eigenspaces. Geometric multiplicity $\ge k$ forces $\lambda$ into the spectrum of every principal submatrix of order $\ge n-k+1$, hence algebraic multiplicity $\ge k$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (or real $A$ with a complex eigenvector matrix)
cards.conclusion: $\exists V$ invertible, $\Lambda$ diagonal with $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ ⇔ $n$ independent eigenvectors ⇔ nondefective; distinct eigenvalues ⇒ diagonalizable
cards.review_note: Real diagonalizability is a real-spectrum statement; complex-eigenvector equivalence is interpreted over complexification. Splitting-field multiplicities are essential.

baseline_audit.informal: $A$ is diagonalizable if $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ with $\Lambda$ diagonal, equivalently it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, equivalently every eigenvalue has equal geometric and algebraic multiplicity (nondefective). $n$ distinct eigenvalues suffice; a direct sum is diagonalizable iff each summand is; two diagonalizations differ by an invertible block-diagonal factor on the eigenspaces. Geometric multiplicity $\ge k$ forces $\lambda$ into the spectrum of every principal submatrix of order $\ge n-k+1$, hence algebraic multiplicity $\ge k$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (or real $A$ with a complex eigenvector matrix)
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\exists V$ invertible, $\Lambda$ diagonal with $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ ⇔ $n$ independent eigenvectors ⇔ nondefective; distinct eigenvalues ⇒ diagonalizable
baseline_audit.review_note: Real diagonalizability is a real-spectrum statement; complex-eigenvector equivalence is interpreted over complexification. Splitting-field multiplicities are essential.

cards.informal: In positive dimension, a commuting family has a common nonzero eigenvector (Lem 1.3.19) and is simultaneously unitarily upper triangularizable; a family of diagonalizable (normal) matrices commutes iff it is simultaneously (unitarily) diagonalizable, with any eigenvalue order for one member; real diagonalizable matrices with real eigenvalues need only a real similarity. For commuting $A,B$ the eigenvalues of $A+B$ and $AB$ are $\alpha_i+\beta_i$ and $\alpha_i\beta_i$ for suitable orderings. Simultaneous triangularization by similarity is equivalent to unitary simultaneous triangularization.
hypotheses: $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ a commuting family
for diagonalization: every member diagonalizable (normal for the unitary version)

cards.informal:
If $Ax=\lambda x$ and $y^*A=\mu y^*$ with $\lambda
e\mu$ then $y^*x=0$. If $y^*x
e0$ for the same $\lambda$ then $A=S([\lambda]\oplus B)S^{-1}$ with $S=[x\ S_1]$ and $S^{-*}e_1=y/(x^*y)$ (and conversely). A simple eigenvalue has $y^*x
e0$; for geometric multiplicity one, simplicity is equivalent to $y^*x
e0$, and $\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I-A)=\gamma xy^*$, $\gamma
e0$. Similarities map right eigenvectors by $S$ and left ones by $S^{-*}$.
cards.conclusion: $\lambda\ne\mu\Rightarrow y^*x=0$; $\lambda$ simple $\Rightarrow y^*x\ne0$ and $A\sim[\lambda]\oplus B$ with spectral projector $xy^*/(y^*x)$

current_atlas_snapshot.informal:
If $Ax=\lambda x$ and $y^*A=\mu y^*$ with $\lambda
e\mu$ then $y^*x=0$. If $y^*x
e0$ for the same $\lambda$ then $A=S([\lambda]\oplus B)S^{-1}$ with $S=[x\ S_1]$ and $S^{-*}e_1=y/(x^*y)$ (and conversely). A simple eigenvalue has $y^*x
e0$; for geometric multiplicity one, simplicity is equivalent to $y^*x
e0$, and $\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I-A)=\gamma xy^*$, $\gamma
e0$. Similarities map right eigenvectors by $S$ and left ones by $S^{-*}$.
current_atlas_snapshot.conclusion: $\lambda\ne\mu\Rightarrow y^*x=0$; $\lambda$ simple $\Rightarrow y^*x\ne0$ and $A\sim[\lambda]\oplus B$ with spectral projector $xy^*/(y^*x)$

cards.informal: $A^k\to0$ iff $\rho(A)<1$; then $\sum_kA^k=(I-A)^{-1}$. $\sup_k\|A^k\|<\infty$ iff $\rho(A)\le1$ and every eigenvalue of modulus one is semisimple. Quantitatively, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon$ with $\|A^k\|\le C_\varepsilon(\rho(A)+\varepsilon)^k$.
cards.conclusion: $\lim_{k\to\infty}A^k=0\iff\rho(A)<1$; power bounded $\iff\rho(A)\le1$ and unimodular eigenvalues semisimple

cards.informal: If $U=\begin{pmatrix}U_{11}&U_{12}\\U_{21}&U_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ is unitary (real orthogonal) with $U_{11}\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$, $p\le q$, there are unitaries $V_1,W_1\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$, $V_2,W_2\in\mathbb C^{q\times q}$ with $(V_1\oplus V_2)^*U(W_1\oplus W_2)=\begin{pmatrix}C&S&0\\-S&C&0\\0&0&I_{q-p}\end{pmatrix}$, $C=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i(U_{11}))$, $S=(I-C^2)^{1/2}$. In particular $\operatorname{rank}U_{12}=\operatorname{rank}U_{21}$ and $\operatorname{rank}U_{22}=\operatorname{rank}U_{11}+n-2p$. An idempotent $P$ with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_g>1$ is unitarily similar to $\bigoplus_i\begin{pmatrix}1&(\sigma_i^2-1)^{1/2}\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus I\oplus0$, so, when $\operatorname{rank}P>0$, $\|P\|=1/\cos\theta_{\max}$ between its range and the orthogonal complement of its null space.

current_atlas_snapshot.informal: If $U=\begin{pmatrix}U_{11}&U_{12}\\U_{21}&U_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ is unitary (real orthogonal) with $U_{11}\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$, $p\le q$, there are unitaries $V_1,W_1\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$, $V_2,W_2\in\mathbb C^{q\times q}$ with $(V_1\oplus V_2)^*U(W_1\oplus W_2)=\begin{pmatrix}C&S&0\\-S&C&0\\0&0&I_{q-p}\end{pmatrix}$, $C=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i(U_{11}))$, $S=(I-C^2)^{1/2}$. In particular $\operatorname{rank}U_{12}=\operatorname{rank}U_{21}$ and $\operatorname{rank}U_{22}=\operatorname{rank}U_{11}+n-2p$. cards.informal: The companion matrix $C_p$ of a monic $p$ has $p$ as both minimal and characteristic polynomial. For $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$: $\deg q_A=n$ ⇔ $q_A=p_A$ ⇔ $A$ nonderogatory (every eigenvalue geometrically simple) ⇔ $A$ is similar to $C_{p_A}$ ⇔ some $b$ has Krylov grade $n$; then every matrix commuting with $A$ is a polynomial in $A$.
cards.conclusion: $\operatorname{minpoly}(C_p)=\operatorname{charpoly}(C_p)=p$; $A$ nonderogatory ⇔ $A\sim C_{p_A}$ ⇔ $\exists b$: $\operatorname{grade}(A,b)=n$
cards.review_note: The actual Frobenius companion has the prescribed monic charpoly and minpoly, and full operator minimal-polynomial degree is equivalent to full-grade vectors, a Krylov companion basis and equality of minimal/characteristic polynomials. Commuting matrices are unique bounded-degree evaluations. The one-dimensional-eigenspace criterion is over a splitting field; the actual real-matrix complexification preserves the minimal-polynomial degree.

clauses.statement: The concrete Frobenius shift-and-negative-coefficients companion of a monic polynomial has that polynomial as both characteristic and minimal polynomial, including the degree-zero polynomial one.

Every finite matrix over any field has a vector realizing its minimal polynomial; full minimal-polynomial degree is equivalent to a full-grade vector and to equality with the characteristic polynomial.

A full-grade vector gives the native basis of successive Krylov powers in which the matrix is its characteristic companion; existence of such a companion basis representation is equivalent to equality of minimal and characteristic polynomials.
For a full-grade vector, every matrix commuting with the operator is the evaluation of a unique polynomial of degree below the dimension, with the zero polynomial in dimension zero.

Over a field where the characteristic polynomial splits, full minimal-polynomial degree is equivalent to a one-dimensional eigenspace for every actual eigenvalue, including repeated eigenvalues and empty dimension.

Field extension preserves the matrix minimal-polynomial degree, so the geometric criterion for a real matrix is correctly equivalent to geometric simplicity of the eigenvalues of its complexification.

baseline_audit.informal: The companion matrix $C_p$ of a monic $p$ has $p$ as both minimal and characteristic polynomial. For $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$: $\deg q_A=n$ ⇔ $q_A=p_A$ ⇔ $A$ nonderogatory (every eigenvalue geometrically simple) ⇔ $A$ is similar to $C_{p_A}$ ⇔ some $b$ has Krylov grade $n$; then every matrix commuting with $A$ is a polynomial in $A$.
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\operatorname{minpoly}(C_p)=\operatorname{charpoly}(C_p)=p$; $A$ nonderogatory ⇔ $A\sim C_{p_A}$ ⇔ $\exists b$: $\operatorname{grade}(A,b)=n$

findings.finding: The geometric criterion must use eigenvalues over a splitting field. For real A two copies of a 2x2 real rotation have no real eigenvalues but minimal degree 2<4. ScalarExtension now proves the correct complexification criterion.

cards.informal: For symmetric $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with decreasing eigenvalues $\lambda_0\ge\dots\ge\lambda_{n-1}$ (`eigenvalues₀`): $\lambda_k(-A)=-\lambda_{n-1-k}(A)$. If $x^\top Ax>c\|x\|^2$ for all nonzero $x$ in a subspace of dimension $k+1$, then $\lambda_k(A)>c$ (strict form of the existing non-strict test); consequently a $k$-dimensional subspace on which $x^\top Ax\ge0$ (resp. $>0$ off $0$) forces at least $k$ nonnegative (resp. positive) eigenvalues.

If $x^\top Ax>c\|x\|^2$ for all nonzero $x$ in a subspace of dimension $k+1$, then $\lambda_k(A)>c$ (strict form of the existing non-strict test); consequently a $k$-dimensional subspace on which $x^\top Ax\ge0$ (resp. $>0$ off $0$) forces at least $k$ nonnegative (resp. positive) eigenvalues.
hypotheses: strict test: $x^\top Ax>c\,x^\top x$ for all $x\in S\setminus\{0\}$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\lambda_k(-A)=-\lambda_{n-1-k}(A)$; $\lambda_k(A)>c$; $\#\{i:\lambda_i(A)\ge0\}\ge k$ (resp. $>0$)

cards.informal: Let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric (increasing order $\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_n$). If $B$ has $\pi$ positive and $\nu$ negative eigenvalues then $\lambda_i(A+B)\le\lambda_{i+\pi}(A)$ and $\lambda_{i-\nu}(A)\le\lambda_i(A+B)$. In particular if $\operatorname{rank}B=r$ then $\lambda_{i-r}(A)\le\lambda_i(A+B)\le\lambda_{i+r}(A)$, and for $z\in\mathbb R^n$: $\lambda_i(A)\le\lambda_i(A+zz^\top)\le\lambda_{i+1}(A)$ and $\lambda_{i-1}(A)\le\lambda_i(A-zz^\top)\le\lambda_i(A)$.
cards.conclusion: $\lambda_{i-\nu}(A)\le\lambda_i(A+B)\le\lambda_{i+\pi}(A)$; rank-one interlacing for $A\pm zz^\top$
cards.review_note: The human sequence is increasing while Lean eigenvalues are decreasing. The index shifts reverse accordingly; the stated endpoint range restrictions are essential.

baseline_audit.informal: Let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric (increasing order $\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_n$). If $B$ has $\pi$ positive and $\nu$ negative eigenvalues then $\lambda_i(A+B)\le\lambda_{i+\pi}(A)$ and $\lambda_{i-\nu}(A)\le\lambda_i(A+B)$. In particular if $\operatorname{rank}B=r$ then $\lambda_{i-r}(A)\le\lambda_i(A+B)\le\lambda_{i+r}(A)$, and for $z\in\mathbb R^n$: $\lambda_i(A)\le\lambda_i(A+zz^\top)\le\lambda_{i+1}(A)$ and $\lambda_{i-1}(A)\le\lambda_i(A-zz^\top)\le\lambda_i(A)$.
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\lambda_{i-\nu}(A)\le\lambda_i(A+B)\le\lambda_{i+\pi}(A)$; rank-one interlacing for $A\pm zz^\top$
baseline_audit.review_note: The human sequence is increasing while Lean eigenvalues are decreasing. The index shifts reverse accordingly; the stated endpoint range restrictions are essential.

cards.informal: If $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ is symmetric positive definite and $B$ symmetric, there is a nonsingular $S$ with $A=SS^\top$ and $B=S\Lambda S^\top$, $\Lambda$ real diagonal whose entries are the eigenvalues of $A^{-1}B$ (and $\Lambda$ has the inertia of $B$). Consequently $A^{-1}B$ (and $AB$) is diagonalisable with real eigenvalues, nonnegative if $B\succeq0$. More generally (Thm 4.5.17) for invertible symmetric $A$, $A,B$ are simultaneously congruent to real diagonals iff $A^{-1}B$ is diagonalisable with real spectrum. A PSD–PSD version holds with $A=S(I_r\oplus0)S^\top$.
cards.conclusion: $A=SS^\top$, $B=S\Lambda S^\top$ with $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda(A^{-1}B))$

current_atlas_snapshot.informal: If $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ is symmetric positive definite and $B$ symmetric, there is a nonsingular $S$ with $A=SS^\top$ and $B=S\Lambda S^\top$, $\Lambda$ real diagonal whose entries are the eigenvalues of $A^{-1}B$ (and $\Lambda$ has the inertia of $B$). Consequently $A^{-1}B$ (and $AB$) is diagonalisable with real eigenvalues, nonnegative if $B\succeq0$. More generally (Thm 4.5.17) for invertible symmetric $A$, $A,B$ are simultaneously congruent to real diagonals iff $A^{-1}B$ is diagonalisable with real spectrum. A PSD–PSD version holds with $A=S(I_r\oplus0)S^\top$.
current_atlas_snapshot.conclusion: $A=SS^\top$, $B=S\Lambda S^\top$ with $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda(A^{-1}B))$

cards.informal: Let $R_i=\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|$, $C_j=\sum_{i\ne j}|a_{ij}|$. (i) A union of $k$ Geršgorin discs disjoint from the remaining $n-k$ contains exactly $k$ eigenvalues; the column discs work too. (ii) $\rho(A)\le\min\{\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|,\max_j\sum_i|a_{ij}|\}$, and with positive weights $\rho(A)\le\max_ip_i^{-1}\sum_jp_j|a_{ij}|$. (iii) If $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant ($|a_{ii}|>R_i$) with positive diagonal, every eigenvalue has positive real part; if moreover $A$ is symmetric it is positive definite. (iv) Taussky: an irreducible weakly diagonally dominant matrix with at least one strictly dominant row is nonsingular (and PD if symmetric with positive diagonal).

baseline_audit.informal: Let $R_i=\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|$, $C_j=\sum_{i\ne j}|a_{ij}|$. (i) A union of $k$ Geršgorin discs disjoint from the remaining $n-k$ contains exactly $k$ eigenvalues; the column discs work too. (ii) $\rho(A)\le\min\{\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|,\max_j\sum_i|a_{ij}|\}$, and with positive weights $\rho(A)\le\max_ip_i^{-1}\sum_jp_j|a_{ij}|$. (iii) If $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant ($|a_{ii}|>R_i$) with positive diagonal, every eigenvalue has positive real part; if moreover $A$ is symmetric it is positive definite. (iv) Taussky: an irreducible weakly diagonally dominant matrix with at least one strictly dominant row is nonsingular (and PD if symmetric with positive diagonal).
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (real symmetric for the PD conclusions)
baseline_audit.conclusion: eigenvalue counts in isolated disc unions; row/column-sum spectral radius bounds; diagonal dominance ⇒ Re λ > 0 / PD

cards.informal: Let $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ be diagonalisable and $E$ arbitrary. Every eigenvalue $\hat\lambda$ of $A+E$ satisfies $\min_i|\hat\lambda-\lambda_i|\le\kappa(V)\,|||E|||$ for any matrix norm induced by an absolute vector norm (e.g. $\|\cdot\|_1,\|\cdot\|_2,\|\cdot\|_\infty$), with $\kappa(V)=|||V|||\,|||V^{-1}|||$. If $A$ is normal, $\min_i|\hat\lambda-\lambda_i|\le\|E\|_2$. Residual form: for $\hat x\ne0$ and $r=A\hat x-\hat\lambda\hat x$, $\min_i|\hat\lambda-\lambda_i|\le\kappa(V)\|r\|/\|\hat x\|$ (and $\le\|r\|_2/\|\hat x\|_2$ for normal $A$).
hypotheses: norm induced by an absolute vector norm
cards.conclusion: $\operatorname{dist}(\hat\lambda,\sigma(A))\le\kappa(V)|||E|||$; residual analogue

cards.informal: Let $\lambda$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$ with right and left eigenvectors $x,y$. Then $y^*x\ne0$, $A$ is similar to $\lambda\oplus A_1$ with $\lambda\notin\sigma(A_1)$, and for every $E$ there is a unique eigenvalue $\lambda(t)$ of $A+tE$ near $\lambda$ for small $|t|$, continuous and differentiable at $0$ with $\lambda'(0)=y^*Ex/y^*x$. For symmetric $A$ with unit eigenvector $x$: $\lambda'(0)=x^\top Ex$.

baseline_audit.informal: Let $\lambda$ be a simple eigenvalue of $A$ with right and left eigenvectors $x,y$. Then $y^*x\ne0$, $A$ is similar to $\lambda\oplus A_1$ with $\lambda\notin\sigma(A_1)$, and for every $E$ there is a unique eigenvalue $\lambda(t)$ of $A+tE$ near $\lambda$ for small $|t|$, continuous and differentiable at $0$ with $\lambda'(0)=y^*Ex/y^*x$. For symmetric $A$ with unit eigenvector $x$: $\lambda'(0)=x^\top Ex$.
hypotheses: $\lambda$ an algebraically simple eigenvalue of $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$
baseline_audit.conclusion: $\lambda'(0)=y^*Ex/(y^*x)$
